lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: be able to draw dot-and-cross diagrams to show electrons in covalent substances, including: i molecules with single, double and triple bonds ii species with dative covalent (coordinate) bonds, including Al 2 Cl 6 and the ammonium ion

primer.text: Shared pairs come in singles, doubles, triples - and donations. Dot-and-cross diagrams track every electron's origin; oxygen doubles up, nitrogen triples, and a lone pair can fund an entire bond to an electron-deficient partner, as ammonia does to H+ and two AlCl3 molecules do to each other. This note drills the diagrams, bond orders and dative cases.

modules.title: Diagrams of the shared deal
modules.opening: Covalent compounds fill outer shells by pooling rather than transferring: each atom contributes electrons to shared pairs, and every partner counts the shared electrons toward a noble-gas arrangement. Dot-and-cross diagrams record the deal - dots for one atom's electrons, crosses for the other's, drawn only in the outer shells.
keyPoints: Atoms in covalent compounds share their outer valence electrons to reach noble gas configurations.
Each shared pair is counted by both atoms toward a full outer shell.
Dot-and-cross diagrams show only outer-shell electrons, with symbols distinguishing each atom's contribution.
Unlike ionic diagrams, covalent drawings need no brackets or corner charges.
The periodic table tells you how many outer electrons each non-metal brings to the deal.

low.restatement: Non-metal atoms lend electrons into joint pairs; both partners count each pair as their own until every shell reads full.
low.analogy: Two students each holding half a library card: neither owns it alone, but together they borrow as one full member.
low.examPointer: Use the periodic table for outer-electron counts - group number gives the contribution each atom brings.

medium.restatement: The shared-pair economy lets each atom claim octet completion without ownership change: dot-and-cross diagrams track the origin of every electron so the examiner can audit the count around each nucleus.
medium.analogy: A joint bank account with colour-coded deposits: the money is shared, but the ledger remembers who paid what in.
medium.examPointer: Audit each atom in your diagram: count dots plus crosses around every nucleus and confirm the octet before moving on.

modules.title: Doubling and tripling up
modules.opening: Some atoms need more than one shared pair to complete their shells. Oxygen gas pairs its atoms with a double bond, carbon dioxide wires each oxygen to carbon doubly, and ethene joins its two carbons doubly. Nitrogen goes one better still: its triple bond pools three pairs between the two atoms.
keyPoints: A double covalent bond shares two pairs of electrons between two atoms.
O2 carries one double bond; CO2 carries two, one to each oxygen; ethene's carbons join by C=C.
A triple covalent bond shares three pairs, as in N2.
Multiple bonds arise when single pairs would leave an atom short of its octet.
Each double bond counts as two shared pairs - four electrons; a triple bond is six.

low.restatement: When one shared pair is not enough, atoms pool two or even three pairs between them - drawing two or three connecting lines.
low.analogy: Handshakes becoming arm-wrestles: two arms locked (double bond) or three ropes tied (triple bond) bind the partners far more tightly.
low.examPointer: Count electrons per bond type aloud: single 2, double 4, triple 6 - the counting is the mark.

medium.restatement: Bond order tracks electron debt: oxygen's six valence electrons need two shared pairs to octet, nitrogen's five need three; CO2 and ethene merely relocate the same double-bond logic into larger frameworks.
medium.analogy: Instalment plans: the bigger the missing share of the octet, the more instalments - pairs - the bond must transfer into the joint account.
medium.examPointer: In diagrams, every bond line equals one pair: audit the count around each atom line by line.

modules.title: The dative bond: one-sided donations
modules.opening: Some bonds are funded by one partner alone. When an atom with a lone pair meets an electron-deficient atom with an unfilled orbital, the whole shared pair can come from the donor - a dative covalent, or coordinate, bond. The ammonium ion is the classic: ammonia's lone pair lands on a bare proton. Aluminium chloride plays the same game twice over, dimerising into Al2Cl6 when two AlCl3 molecules swap lone-pair donations.
keyPoints: A dative covalent bond forms when a lone pair is donated to an electron-deficient atom.
An electron-deficient atom has an unfilled outer orbital.
In a dative bond both shared electrons come from the same donor atom.
Ammonia donates its lone pair to H+ to form the ammonium ion, NH4+.
Two AlCl3 molecules dimerise to Al2Cl6 at lower temperatures via two chlorine-to-aluminium coordinate bonds.

low.restatement: Normally each partner funds half a bond; in a dative bond one atom funds the whole pair and hands it to a partner with a spare slot.
low.analogy: Buying a cinema seat for a friend who arrived cashless: the seat is shared, but one wallet paid for it.
low.examPointer: Arrow notation points from donor to acceptor - draw the arrow head on the electron-deficient atom.

medium.restatement: Dative bonding repairs octet deficits pair-by-pair: the donor's lone pair fills the acceptor's empty orbital, converting AlCl3's electron poverty at low temperature into a four-coordinate dimer held by two coordinate links.
medium.analogy: A key-cutting kiosk (donor) slotting a spare key (lone pair) into a friend's empty lock (unfilled orbital) - the door then opens for both.
medium.examPointer: State the temperature condition for AlCl3: monomer at high temperature, dimer Al2Cl6 at lower temperature.

glossary.definition: A bond sharing two pairs of electrons - four electrons - between two atoms, drawn as two lines.
A bond sharing three pairs of electrons - six in total - as in N2.
A coordinate bond whose shared pair comes entirely from one donor atom's lone pair.
Describing an atom with an unfilled outer orbital, ready to accept a donated pair.
